seite.titel: IYAMBAE Tuner — Spotify in 432 Hz, without converting a file
seite.beschreibung: Menu-bar app for macOS. Retunes your entire system audio in real time — 432 Hz, historical concert pitches or any value you choose, with no change of tempo and no converting. Windows and Linux are built and on their way. We promise you no effect. We give you a slider.

auf.titel: Spotify in 432 Hz. Without converting a single file.
auf.vorwort: Netflix, YouTube, your own player just the same. The Tuner sits in the system audio — not in the file.
probe.hilfe: Music on, then drag from 440 to 432.
probe.schirm.aria: Display: shows the beating between the reference tone and the chosen concert pitch as a pulsing waveform.
probe.ohne.1: The test needs JavaScript. But what it is about can also be worked out on paper:
probe.ohne.2: 440 minus 432 is eight hertz. Two tones eight hertz apart cancel each other out eight times a second — that pulsing is what you hear, and it is how people have tuned instruments for centuries: you wait until it stops.
probe.ohne.3: The Tuner does to your whole system audio what the slider here does to two tones.
probe.fuss: Chopin, Nocturne op. 9 no. 2 — public domain. It is retuned here by the same signal core that sits in the Tuner, and at its best setting: the pitch moves, the tempo stays put. That is why it says 100 %, wherever you drag. The display assumes the recording sits at 440 — the Tuner on your own machine does not assume, it measures.

fragen.vorwort: There for whoever asks. Out of the way for whoever wants to download.
frage.hz.1: A concert pitch. It fixes where A4 sits, and everything else follows from it. The standard says 440 Hz; 432 Hz lies eight hertz below that, which is −31.77 cents, or just under a third of a semitone.
frage.hz.2: The Tuner shifts the whole sound by exactly that distance. It does not pick out single notes, and it changes nothing about the music except its pitch.
frage.440.titel: So where does 440 Hz come from?
frage.440.1: From an agreement, not from nature. When Alexander J. Ellis gathered five hundred years of European tuning pitches in 1885, his table ran from 370 to 567 Hz — more than a fifth of spread. The reason was banal: organ pipes were built to the local measure of length, and the “foot” in France was not the “foot” in Saxony. Between the Paris tuning fork of 1822 at 432 Hz and the one of 1855 at 449 Hz lie thirty-three years — and the same city.
frage.440.2: 440 comes from 1834, proposed by Johann Heinrich Scheibler, a silk manufacturer from Krefeld. His reason was as unspectacular as it gets: 440 was the mean around which Viennese pianos drifted between warmth and cold. The conference that turned it into a world standard in 1939 met at BBC headquarters and preferred 440 to 439 because 439 is a prime number and could not be produced from the BBC’s quartz oscillator by chains of dividers.
skala.titel: Concert pitch A4 through the centuries
skala.gross.aria: Scale of tuning pitches from 400 to 480 hertz with four marks: Baroque 415, Scheibler 1834 and London 1939 at 440, Paris tuning fork 1855 at 449, Highland bagpipe 470 to 480.
skala.415: Historically informed performance, one semitone lower
skala.aus.unter: this is where it all happens today
skala.aus.aria: Enlarged detail from 430 to 450 hertz: Milan 1881 at 432, diapason normal Paris 1859 at 435, the standard 440, Germany and Austria today 443, Berlin Philharmonic under Karajan 445.
skala.liste.415: Historically informed performance — exactly one semitone lower
skala.liste.432: Milan 1881 — Verdi argued for 435 and let 432 stand
brief.zitat: “A piece of childishness that would almost lay itself open to ridicule.”
brief.quelle: Giuseppe Verdi to Arrigo Boito, 8 November 1885. Boito represented Italy at the Vienna pitch conference. Verdi held the 864 vibrations — that is, 432 Hz — to be the more correct ones, but insisting on them would have struck him as ridiculous; the main purpose was one single pitch for everyone. Uniformity mattered more to him than the number. We see it much the same way — and therefore leave the number to you.
frage.forschung.1: A randomised comparison of 432 against 443 Hz — that is, against the tuning today’s orchestras really play at. 43 people, each hearing both. At 432 the pulse fell by three beats a minute, at 443 by one. Pulse wave velocity fell only at 432. The difference between the two tunings held up statistically. The authors themselves write, though, that they cannot say whether this is down to the number 432 or simply to its being lower.
frage.forschung.2: Aravena et al. (2020) compared 432 Hz, 440 Hz and silence before a tooth extraction; 42 people. For anxiety both music groups worked equally well — no difference between 432 and 440. The much-quoted cortisol finding does not survive a check against the full text: the 432 group started out at half the level of the others, and the change was not statistically sound in any of the three groups.
frage.forschung.3: And what speaks against it, so you don’t hear it elsewhere first: these are small studies, no meta-analysis, no independent replication. In the same trial that measured the pulse, the psychological scores did not differ between 432 and 443. And Jebabli et al. (2025) found 440 better for an athletic warm-up.
frage.forschung.4: What follows from that: something has been measured, and it is little. We promise you nothing. Until 01.09.2026 a cortisol figure stood here that we had taken from a study’s abstract. Checking the full text did not bear it out — and then you correct it instead of leaving it standing. The full texts are below under “What others write about it” — read them yourself instead of believing us. And then listen. The only measurement that counts for you, you make with your own ears.
frage.digital.1: A widespread picture shows a smooth wave on the left and a staircase on the right. Almost everyone reads it as: digital is jagged. The picture is correct — it just doesn’t show the end.
frage.digital.aria: Three panels: a smooth wave on the left, the same wave as dots with a staircase in the middle, a smooth wave again on the right.
frage.digital.2: The staircase is the intermediate form. On playback a filter sits behind the converter, and it turns the points back into a continuous curve. Below the limit frequency there is exactly one smooth curve through those points.
frage.digital.3: What digital really loses is smaller and duller: a noise floor from the rounding, at 16 bit some 96 decibels below the signal — quieter than the surface noise of any record. Add filter ringing and jitter, audible only in badly built gear.
frage.digital.4: We write this even though it contradicts our own feeling. Anyone who says vinyl sounds different is right — it just isn’t the staircase. It is the cut, the distortion that breathes with the music, and the fact that you can’t play a record in passing.
frage.medizin.1: No. The IYAMBAE Tuner is not a medical device, not a remedy and not a therapeutic instrument. It is a tool that shifts pitch.
frage.medizin.2: It is not intended to detect, treat or alleviate any illness, and we claim that nowhere. If something is wrong with you, see a doctor.
frage.528.titel: What about 528 Hz and the Solfeggio frequencies?
frage.528.1: 528 Hz is not a concert pitch but a single note — roughly a C5. A concert pitch fixes A4, and everything else follows from it. The Tuner shifts the whole sound by an interval; it does not set a single note.
frage.528.2: It can still be worked out: if you want your C5 at 528 Hz, you set A4 to 444.0 Hz — the slider can do that. At A4 = 432 Hz the same C5 sits at about 513.7 Hz.
frage.528.3: About the Solfeggio series itself we say nothing. We know of no source on it that we could pass on here in good conscience, and so we claim neither that it does something nor that it does not.
frage.systeme.1: macOS 14.4 and up — the complete app in the menu bar. Linux with PipeWire 0.3.60 and up — recently with a tray icon as well: pitches under their names, on and off, choice of engine, start at login. Underneath, a LADSPA plugin works in the filter chain. Demonstrated over D-Bus, the click measured: “Verdi tuning” → 432.331 Hz at the output device. Built for Debian 13; for Ubuntu and Zorin it has to be rebuilt.
frage.systeme.2: Under GNOME the tray icon needs the AppIndicator extension once. The package recommends it, and the program says so at startup — instead of staying invisible and leaving the impression that nothing had been installed.
frage.systeme.3: Windows: files yes, system audio not yet. There is its own window, a tray icon and an installer that needs no administrator rights. What it can retune there is files. Not the running system audio — the virtual output device for that is missing.
frage.systeme.4: The reason for this order is technical: Windows lets system audio be listened in on, but not replaced. Anyone who wants to genuinely replace it has to become the output device. On macOS the capture interface does that; on Linux, PipeWire’s filter chain. On Windows it takes a virtual device — a driver of our own is the next step.
frage.telefon.1: Because that is where the sandbox draws its line, not where the effort runs out. On iOS there is no counterpart in any form. On Android you may only capture someone else’s audio if the playing app permits it — and Spotify, Netflix and YouTube do not.
frage.telefon.2: What would be possible is something else: a player of our own that takes the music in hand itself. That is being thought about.
frage.webseite.titel: Why an app and not simply a website?
frage.webseite.1: Because a website has to guess and the app can measure. A page in the browser assumes the recording lies at 440 Hz, calculates the fixed factor 432⁄440 and applies it to everything. With a recording that lies at 443 — the value common in Germany today — you end up at 435 instead of 432.
frage.webseite.2: The Tuner determines the actual tuning of the running sound and works out the distance to the target from that. What lies at 443 is shifted 443 → 432, not 440 → 432. And it reaches the system audio, not just one tab.
frage.webseite.w1.was: That is how far the time-stretch factor is from unity. For an octave it would be 50 %.
frage.webseite.w2.was: The tempo stays. Simply playing back more slowly would turn 120 BPM into 117.8.
frage.webseite.w3.was: of one core with the fast engine — 1077 times real time, measured on Windows.
frage.webseite.w4.was: allocations in the real-time callback. Not claimed: the build script takes the DLL apart and lists every call that leads out. There are none.
frage.latenz.titel: How much latency does it cost?
frage.latenz.1: Shifting pitch without touching tempo costs time — and how much depends on the method. You choose.
frage.latenz.w1.was: Delay line. Fast enough for video and for playing along. The sound stays on the lips.
frage.latenz.w2.was: High Quality (Signalsmith). Sounds better, but is useless with video — a quarter of a second of offset is visible.
frage.latenz.2: The switch crossfades over 25 ms so that the change does not click.
frage.radio.titel: What has this got to do with the radio?
frage.radio.1: If the Tuner is running on the same computer, IYAMBAE Radio can notice it and switch off its own guessing retune. Then the app that measures takes over.
frage.radio.2: You are asked twice in the process: the page asks once, and the Tuner asks you. Without your consent no website learns that you are using it — not even that it is installed. A list of permitted websites in the program code would have been more convenient. It would only have answered the wrong question.
frage.preis.1: This test release costs nothing. It asks for no account, no email address and no payment details — you download a file, and that is that.
frage.preis.2: Nothing has been decided about a price for a later, finished version. If that changes, it will say so here.
frage.daten.1: This page sets no cookies, measures nothing and loads nothing from other people’s servers. The fonts sit on the same server as the page — a link to a font collection in the USA would send your IP address there before you had clicked on anything.
frage.daten.2: The Tuner needs no account and sends nothing away. It processes the sound on the computer itself and records it nowhere. The only interface to the outside is the service for the radio on 127.0.0.1 — it does not leave your computer and answers only if you allow it.
frage.daten.3: The details are in the privacy policy.
wege.vorwort: There are three ways to enjoy 432 Hz. They do not exclude each other — they answer different questions.
wege.1.was: Computers only. Every app, every service, without touching a single file.
wege.1.stand: Where we stand: we are waiting for Apple’s Developer ID. It cannot go into the App Store — it sits too deep in the system for that. Through this site it can.
wege.2.titel: 2 Players that convert as they play
wege.2.was: With any DRM-free source, on the phone too. The catch: you have to own the music and have it stored somewhere.
wege.2.stand: For radio, iyambae.fm covers that need for now. Our own player is planned — but only once we know what we can do differently and better.
wege.3.was: Only with DRM-free material, and honestly only worth it for “lossless”: .flac or .wav.
wege.3.stand: What was once heavily compressed would have to be compressed a second time when converted. With “lossless” the sound is recalculated once — but not compressed a second time. That is the difference.
wege.schluss: For now the focus is on the Tuner and the website. After the test phase we want to offer the software at a fair price. It is time everyone had the freedom to hear music in the tuning they chose themselves. If that isn’t possible in daily life — telephones, doorbells, church bells, sirens, shop music — then at least on your own devices.

hoer.seite.titel: Can you hear the difference between 432 and 440 Hz? — blind test
hoer.seite.beschreibung: A blind test in two rounds: first 432 against 440 Hz, then 432 against 433. The same excerpt, random order, five trials. You find out what you really hear — and what the number has to do with it. Free, no account.
hoer.vorwort: The same excerpt twice, tuned differently, the order shuffled. You say which one sounds lower. Five trials per round — and at the end it says what the result is worth.
hoer.hinweis.start: Listen to both — as often as you like. Headphones help; laptop speakers barely reproduce low notes.
hoer.wie.titel: What is measured here — and what is not
hoer.wie.r1.text: 31.8 cents apart — just under a third of a semitone. The threshold at which people tell two pitches apart in direct comparison is around 3 to 12 cents. Almost everyone passes this round, and that is not imagination but physics.
hoer.wie.r2.text: 4.0 cents — at the threshold. This round answers the real question: does the number 432 have a sound of its own, or do you only hear that something is lower? Anyone who experiences 432 as special ought to be able to tell it from 433.
hoer.wie.sauber.text: Both excerpts run through the same signal core — the 440 one too, at factor 1.0. Otherwise you would hear the processing instead of the pitch, and that would be the real giveaway.
hoer.wie.sauber.pegel: The loudness difference is measured and comes to 0.03 dB between 432 and 440, and 0.01 dB between 432 and 433. That is far below anything a person hears — so there is nothing to give it away but the pitch itself. Loudness is the commonest quiet cheat in listening tests: people take the louder one for the better one.
hoer.wie.sauber.zufall: The order is shuffled anew for every trial, and the scoring says what small numbers are worth: five out of five by pure guessing happens 3.1 % of the time, four out of five or better 18.8 %.
hoer.wie.ehrlich.titel: What a result does not prove
hoer.wie.ehrlich.text: Five trials are five trials. Anyone who gets them all in round 2 may have a very fine ear — or may have been lucky. And anyone who misses does not therefore hear badly: 4 cents is too little for almost everyone. The test says something about this afternoon, not about you.
hoer.wie.ehrlich.geschmack: And it says nothing about which one you prefer. That is a different question, it is a matter of taste, and only you can answer it.
hoer.danach.text: If you want to know what your own music sits on, measure it — free, in your browser, nothing is uploaded. And if you want to hear it differently for good, that is what the IYAMBAE Tuner does: for everything coming out of your speakers, without touching a file.
hoer.wort.start: Listen to both — as often as you like.
hoer.wort.fehler: The sound cannot be prepared in this browser. Try a different one.
hoer.wort.zufallSatz: That well or better comes up by blind guessing {p} % of the time.
hoer.wort.r1gut: You hear 31.8 cents — just under a third of a semitone. You are not imagining it. Almost everyone passes this round.
hoer.wort.r1mau: Almost everyone passes this round. If it goes wrong here it is usually the speakers — try headphones.
hoer.wort.r2gut: Four cents. That is remarkable — and rare. Over five trials it may also have been luck; the number below says how often.
hoer.wort.r2mau: The difference is audible. The exact number is not. Four cents lie below the threshold for almost everyone — and that is the honest finding: you hear that something is lower. That it is exactly 432.0 is heard by nobody.
mess.seite.titel: What pitch is my music tuned to? — measure it free
mess.seite.beschreibung: Drop a music file into the window and find out what concert pitch it really sits on — 432, 440, 443 Hz or somewhere between. The maths runs in your browser: your file never leaves your machine. Free, no account, no uploading.
mess.titel: What concert pitch is your music on?
mess.vorwort: Drag a file here. In a few seconds you will know what the recording is really tuned to — and how far that is from 432 Hz.
mess.zone.klein: MP3, M4A, WAV, FLAC, OGG — whatever your browser can play
mess.bruecke.text: This page tells you what your music sits on. The IYAMBAE Tuner changes it — for everything coming out of your speakers: Spotify, YouTube, your own player, without touching a single file. And it measures the same way, instead of assuming 440.
mess.hoertest: And if you want to know what your ears can do: in the blind test you hear the same passage twice, tuned differently, and guess — five trials, with honest scoring.
mess.frage.hochladen.text: No. The maths runs in your browser, on your device. The file is not transmitted, not buffered and not stored. You can disconnect from the network once this page has loaded — the measuring keeps working.
mess.frage.kammerton.text: Concert pitch is the reference tone a piece is tuned to — given as the frequency of the A above middle C. 440 Hz is the usual value today, set in 1955 by the standard ISO 16. Anyone listening at 432 Hz has their material tuned about 1.8 per cent lower: 31.8 cents, just under a third of a semitone.
mess.frage.abweichung.titel: Why isn’t my music on 440 Hz?
mess.frage.abweichung.text: Because almost no recording sits exactly there. Orchestras today often tune to 442 or 443 Hz, historical performance practice to 415, older tapes have changed speed over decades, and digitising either corrects for it or does not. The 440 are a standard, not a law of nature.
mess.frage.genau.text: On pure tones from 432 to 445 Hz the error stays below 0.2 cents, on real music below 1 cent — checked against recordings we detuned on purpose, so the truth was known. A cent is one hundredth of a semitone; people tell apart five to ten at best.
mess.frage.genau.wie: The maths works on the peaks in the frequency spectrum: every tone is asked how far it sits from the nearest equal-tempered step, and all of them together give a circular mean — circular, because +49 and −51 cents are the same tuning. It is the same method the IYAMBAE Tuner uses to estimate the source pitch.
mess.frage.grenze.titel: What can this measurement not do?
mess.frage.grenze.text: It only identifies the tuning to within a semitone. Baroque pitch 415.3 Hz sits exactly one semitone below 440 — to the maths both look the same, and it reports 440. That is not a weakness of the method but lies in the matter itself: a semitone lower is the same tuning, just a different key. Anyone measuring historical recordings has to keep that in mind.
mess.frage.grenze.mehr: And it needs tones. With pure percussion, speech or noise the readings cancel each other out — then the page reports a low confidence instead of an invented number.
mess.frage.sicherheit.titel: What does the confidence percentage mean?
mess.frage.sicherheit.text: It says how much the samples from the piece agree. We measure at up to 24 places spread across the whole piece and compare them. From 35 per cent the estimate counts as sound — with clean musical material it is usually above 90. If it falls below, the page says so explicitly.
mess.frage.formate.text: Anything your browser can play: MP3, M4A/AAC, WAV, FLAC, OGG, Opus. The soundtrack of a video too, if you drop the video file in. Very long files take a moment — the measuring is still spread across the whole piece, not just the beginning.
mess.wort.fehlerLesen: Your browser cannot read this file. Try MP3, M4A, WAV or FLAC.
mess.wort.zuKurz: The recording is too short to measure.
mess.wort.keinKlang: There is no tone here that would have a tuning.
mess.wort.satzUnsicher: No tuning is discernible here — the readings contradict each other.
mess.wort.satzFern: The nearest is {kammerton} Hz ({name}), but {cent} cents off.
mess.wort.warnUnsicher: The confidence is below 35 per cent. With percussion, speech or a very dense arrangement this number does not hold — try another recording.
